title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
author: Nick McMillan
content:
When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got
hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that
it would be sharing the pain with its customers.

The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its
executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier
this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of
sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different
recipients:

Its own leaders.

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using
their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally
covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses,
according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and
earnings calls for publicly traded companies.

Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores
TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.

Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money
other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to
determine executive bonuses.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting
the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has
denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of
these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded
companies.

Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example,
“returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they
generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future
increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because
they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.

But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the
help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said
they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of
them deal with other businesses, not consumers.** **

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because
it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was
a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a
corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s
so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to
think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it
back.”

The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of
Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency
over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new
tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and
China.

Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the
U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it
exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose
Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100
countries.

> “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.”
>
> Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University

Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year
when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed
congressional approval to impose them.

That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund
billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53
million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an
online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called
the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and
consumers who took a hit downstream.

The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which [analyzed the prices of a broad swath
of
goods,](http://newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr1201.pdf)
found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a [study
from Harvard Business School](https://www.library.hbs.edu/working-
knowledge/tariffs-leave-consumers-and-companies-splitting-the-tab) put the
estimate at 43%. One [study
estimated](https://taxfoundation.org/research/federal-tax/trump-tariffs-trade-
war/) that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last
year.

The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies
use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the
Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators [wrote to the
president](https://www.welch.senate.gov/welch-warren-booker-slam-trump-on-
illegal-tariff-theft-from-the-middle-class-demand-plan-for-refunds-directly-
to-consumers-and-small-businesses/), asking if he would require companies to
pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those
that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and
Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that
amounts to theft from the middle class.”

Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted
in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness
of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American
people won’t see it,” [he said](https://www.c-span.org/clip/public-affairs-
event/user-clip-bessent-on-chance-of-tariff-refund-i-got-a-feeling-the-
american-people-wont-see-it/5193762) in February at an Economic Club of Dallas
event.

Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the
tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are
responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.

“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this
administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at
a [press
conference](https://www.threads.com/@mediaite/video/DcUT8cDE4gi/video-
treasury-secretary-scott-bessent-called-targets-billion-tariff-refund-
corporate/). “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark,
‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money
in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”

> “I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money.
>
> Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some
of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these
companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers.
Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging
components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it
have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts
suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that
itemize tariff costs.

Shipping companies, like
[UPS](https://www.ups.com/us/en/shipping/international-
shipping/tariffs/tariff-refunds) and [FedEx](https://ieepa-
refunds.fedex.com/), have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds.
Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on
behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The
companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing
them.

A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to
consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued,
including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike
and Lululemon. [Apparel and leather
costs](https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/how-supreme-courts-ieepa-ruling-and-
new-section-122-tariffs-reshape-costs-across-industries) were some of the
hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether
these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that
businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they
needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures.

One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker
that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named
plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact
wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the
lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well.

“Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to
recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-
inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.”

On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was
raising prices because of the tariffs.

![A man in a suit and wearing a microphone headset gestures while giving a
talk.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2297384892.jpg?w=2560)Chris Nelson,
president and CEO of Stanley Black & Decker Jeff Kowalsky/Bloomberg via Getty
Images

The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on
dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told
shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility.
“Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated
with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an [earnings
call](https://s29.q4cdn.com/245094436/files/doc_financials/2024/q3/SWK-3Q24-Earnings-
Call-Transcript.pdf). Then, a few months after Trump unveiled his tariffs,
Allan said his team was “remaining focused on executing our robust plan
designed to mitigate tariffs” that [he
said](https://s29.q4cdn.com/245094436/files/doc_financials/2025/q2/SWK-2Q25-Earnings-
Call-Transcript.pdf) included “targeted pricing actions to improve our gross
margin.” Later that year, his successor as chief executive, Chris Nelson,
[described more price
hikes](https://s29.q4cdn.com/245094436/files/doc_financials/2025/q3/SWK-3Q25-Earnings-
Call-Transcript.pdf): “We are implementing a second price increase during the
fourth quarter to maintain our innovation and brand investments, given the
pressures resulting from tariff-related cost increases.”

In its more recent disclosures, the company has been vague about how much of
its refund was going to executives, simply saying that some of that gain “was
partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive
compensation.” “Incentive compensation” is a term the toolmaker uses to
describe bonuses.

The company has not responded to the allegations in the lawsuit brought by the
Wisconsin resident and did not answer ProPublica’s questions about who is
getting paid the bonuses, how much they’re worth and whether customers should
be reimbursed.

Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures for ProPublica said it
appeared the windfall boosted the company’s profits, which factor into
formulas that help determine bonus pay for executives and other employees.

“It wasn't the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their
compensation go up?” Germain, the corporate law professor said. “This is one
of many examples where these formulas don't do what they should do.”

The company’s leaders, securities experts said, could have given money back to
consumers or lowered prices. Retail giant Burlington Stores, formerly known as
Burlington Coat Factory, appears to have done just that.

[CEO Michael O’Sullivan recently
said](https://www.burlingtoninvestors.com/news-releases/news-release-
details/burlington-stores-reports-strong-second-quarter-sales-and) the company
got $55 million in tariff refunds and “rather than taking a one-time boost to
earnings” the company plans “to deliver even sharper values to our shoppers,”

“Over the last few years, the rising cost of living has made life difficult
for many customers,” O’Sullivan said, adding that the coming discounts meant
investors should expect the “direct impact of tariff refunds to be neutral.”

A company spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that none of its tariff refund
will be going to bonuses.

Not so for other companies.

![The entrance to a Burlington store in a mall is busy with people coming and
going or hanging around outside the door.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2248291841.jpg?w=2560)Burlington Stores
CEO Michael O’Sullivan says that the company plans to use its tariff refunds
to lower costs for consumers. Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Acushnet, the Massachusetts golf equipment company that includes the brand
Titleist,
[disclosed](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1672013/000167201326000181/golf-20260930.htm)
an “incentive compensation expense of approximately $12.0 million” out of its
refund. Acushnet declined to respond to questions from ProPublica.

TJX, the Massachusetts parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, said it got
back $331 million, but as a result, it “accrued incremental expenses of $112
million for year-end [incentive
compensation](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/109198/000010919826000045/tjxq2fy27earningspressrele.htm)
and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally.”

The company declined to answer questions from ProPublica about how far down
the chain of command the bonuses would go and how much of them would be
reserved for top managers. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not
reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout
beyond this,” a spokesperson said. The company also declined to say whether it
would lower prices or pay back customers with the rest of its refund, saying
only that “the remaining amount will be used to support our future growth.”

ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded
companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None
of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said
they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their
refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such
information.

Nick Guest, an accounting professor at Cornell University who has studied
executive compensation, said the argument for granting leaders bonuses based
on the tariff refunds could go both ways.

“If they were penalized for something out of their control,” he said,
referring to earnings hits caused by Trump’s tariffs last year, rewarding them
now “seems reasonable.”

“But you could say the same thing about customers. If they were penalized,
then is it reasonable that they're not getting rewarded now?” Guest asked. The
companies, he said, are “not obligated to give refunds or reduce prices, but
doing so could certainly build goodwill with customers.”

### How We Used Artificial Intelligence to Find Tariff Refunds

ProPublica searched through securities filings and earnings calls of publicly
traded companies, using key phrases to isolate companies that mentioned
refunds for the Trump administration tariffs that were struck down by the
Supreme Court. We then used an open-weight AI model to make a first pass at
classifying how refunds were being used, including if they were going toward
bonuses or to refunds for customers. For the companies we highlighted in our
reporting, ProPublica reporters reviewed disclosure filings and other records
by hand, looking at context both within documents and across other records to
make sure the results of our analysis were accurate.

The post [Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than
Reimbursing Consumers](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-tariff-
refunds-corporate-bonuses) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
